💡 Key Takeaways
  • The FIA began the Las Vegas Grand Prix weekend by announcing that all manufacturers have agreed to the framework to bring turbocharged V8 engines back to F1 and move away from the current V6 turbo.
  • This move has long been expected, with hopes that it will make engine building easier and cheaper while bringing back the sound that motorsport fans deeply miss.
  • The sound of the V8 engines was a rally cry for fans and has been sorely missed by audiences worldwide.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The FIA began the Las Vegas Grand Prix weekend by announcing that all manufacturers have agreed to the framework to bring turbocharged V8 engines back to F1 and move away from the current V6 turbo.

This move has long been expected, with hopes that it will make engine building easier and cheaper while bringing back the sound that motorsport fans deeply miss.

The sound of the V8 engines was a rally cry for fans and has been sorely missed by audiences worldwide.

The F1 engine manufacturers agreed to a rough-out overarching proposal to move to a 2.1-liter turbocharged V8 from 2030 onwards, with a lower charge of electrical power reducing the hybrid output from 350kW to 200kW, a decrease of nearly 56 percent.

The FIA announced that ‘The plan is to marry the V8 power unit to a chassis which will also be lighter, more agile and placing greater emphasis on driver skill and close racing.”.

With everyone in agreement, PU manufacturers will start to jockey between improving the newly introduced car entering a sophomore season of new regulations and game planning for the major change coming just three seasons down the line.

It’s been 13 years since manufacturers last built a V8 engine for F1.

“This agreement marks a significant milestone in shaping the future of Formula 1,” FIA President Mohammed Ben Sulayem remarked. “From the outset, I have been clear in my ambition to deliver a sport that is more competitive and more exciting for our fans, while remaining at the forefront of innovation and sustainability.

“The return of V8 engines represents an opportunity to reconnect with the DNA of this Championship, bringing back the sound, emotion and pure racing that is loved worldwide. Our vision is clear, lighter, simpler and more affordable cars that put driver skill at the heart of the competition.”.

Victoria Beaver is a nomadic sports writer who spends her time hopping between race tracks and hippie farms. She’s covered every corner of motorsports that will let her in from 410 Sprints to NASCAR to Supercross. Her daily driver is a 2010 Subaru that she refused to do the smallest amount of preventative maintenance on. Instead, she spends her free time and money building a 42-foot Skoolie to one day travel the country full time.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Battlefield 6’s Season 2 was recently pushed back by a month to give Battlefield Studios time to polish up its content.
  • Industry observers note that as discussed in the initial delay message, BF Studios wants the community’s involvement earlier and more consistently in the development of future content.
  • According to recent reports, the first Battlefield Labs session kicking off soon will focus on Contaminated, one of the newly introduced maps coming to Battlefield 6 with Season 2.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Battlefield 6’s Season 2 was recently pushed back by a month to give Battlefield Studios time to polish up its content. Now, the developer has revealed how it plans to use some of that time, and the first port of call is Battlefield Labs.

Industry observers note that as discussed in the initial delay message, BF Studios wants the community’s involvement earlier and more consistently in the development of future content. This includes Season 2, of course, and a big component of what it’s bringing to the game is headed to Labs.

According to recent reports, the first Battlefield Labs session kicking off soon will focus on Contaminated, one of the newly introduced maps coming to Battlefield 6 with Season 2. BF Studios says the map falls between Eastwood and Mirak Valley, in terms of size.

The blog post even likened it to Battlefield 1’s St. Quentin Scar, and Battlefield 5’s Arras. Although we’ve yet to actually play it, the size and description do sound really well, especially in a game as starved of big maps as Battlefield 6 right now is.

Another thing BF Studios wants to test is the way ground vehicle gameplay and aerial presence interact with infantry combat, which is pretty standard for most Battlefield maps. Interestingly, there appears to be some sort of mechanic unique to Contaminated that the developer also wants to evaluate.

Recent findings suggest that more Labs sessions are planned, including one that will show off newly introduced gameplay tools and vehicles. The AH-6 Little Bird helicopter was specifically namedropped, which makes sense given that it’s going to be part of Season 2’s content.

Battlefield Labs sessions will also extend beyond the biggest-ticket items of maps and vehicles. BF Studios said we should expect tests of upcoming features, like the Aircraft Radar, as part of a list of other air combat updates.

Ground vehicles, and they way the various rockets interact with them, will also be evaluated in a different session, with specific adjustments planned for RPGs and TOWs. And, of course, the work to improve and perfect hit reg remains ongoing, and future tweaks will go through Labs first.

Sources indicate that there’s even more exciting news for fans of significant maps, as the blog post also confirmed that Battlefield 4’s Golmud Railway is at the moment in the works, planned to go live in a future season. Golmud Railway will show up early in Labs, and you can expect it to evolve over multiple sessions.

For context, when it does arrive in Battlefield 6, Golmud Railway will be the largest map in the game, which is saying something. Though the map is beloved by vehicle players, it has its problems elsewhere, and BF Studios says it will be looking at all that when it creates the BF6, emphasising that it won’t be a simple port of the BF4 original.

According to recent reports, finally, the post throws a bone to Redsec battle royale players still waiting for a Solo mode. BF Studios continues to test the idea internally, but it’s taking a while. Needless to say, there are so many aspects that need to be considered. Game pace, balance, player survivability, match flow just to name a few.

Redsec BR was built with squads in mind, so that task is extra challenging. Though the developer didn’t say when we can expect Solos to arrive in Labs, players will get a chance to experience it before it enters the live game.

This EV-Swapped 1967 Porsche 912 Has 300 HP And A Split Battery Pack

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that inverted is a name that's been around for a while in the EV-swap world.
  • According to Piston Heads, the owner of this specific 912 had already swapped a more potent 911 engine into its rear end, but wanted something even better suited for daily driving.
  • Industry observers note that there's some clever engineering here, too.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that inverted is a name that's been around for a while in the EV-swap world. It started out doing electric powertrain swaps for classic Range Rovers, which it still does. But it also has a bespoke program now, under which it will develop custom EV swaps for customers for any sort of car they want. In this specific case, Inverted stuffed some batteries and an electric motor into an old Porsche 912. Interestingly, this is the third powertrain that's been in this Porsche.

According to Piston Heads, the owner of this specific 912 had already swapped a more potent 911 engine into its rear end, but wanted something even better suited for daily driving. So they took their car to Inverted and the team got to work. The end result is a car that looks exactly like a normal Porsche 912, with all of its gorgeous old-school styling, but drives like a modern EV.

Industry observers note that there's some clever engineering here, too. The 62 kWh battery pack is more than enough to propel the vintage Porsche's featherweight body a fair ways. However, that's a lot of weight to hang over the rear axle. Air-cooled Porsches were already prone to lift-off oversteer, so they don't need any more. So Inverted came up with an interesting solution: split the pack into two parts. On section is mounted out back where the engine used to be, and the other is under the hood. It means the electric 912's weight balance is actually better than the original car's.

Industry observers note that inverted claims that this EV 912 has around 250 miles of range, and it can DC fast charge at 75 kW. The latter might seem weak in the world of modern EVs, but it's perfectly fine in a classic like this. This is a daily driver, not a long-distance cruiser. So 250 miles is more than enough for daily usage, and plugging it in overnight to charge will get the owner a fresh battery in the morning.

The rear-mounted electric motor makes 300 horsepower, so it's much more potent than the original 912 four-cylinder engine which made around 90 horsepower. Inverted indicates it can hit 0-60 mph in four seconds, which kicks the ass of the stock vehicle. The original 912 took about 13 seconds.

This isn't just a powertrain swap, either. Its interior is completely redone and it's gorgeous. The gauges look like vintage Porsche gauges but they're modified for EV used. For example, the classic Porsche central tachometer was replaced with a power percentage gauge. The fuel gauge is now an analog battery charge gauge, too. It's just lovely.

Recent findings suggest that this is an awesome project and one that would make for an incredible daily driver. It has modern Porsche levels of performance, with modern EV levels of range, in a stylish vintage package. Seems perfect.

#86948. Industry News: I ride e-bikes for a living. This is the real gear I actually use

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 19m • 📚 Deep Dive (3756 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Electrek ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: I ride e-bikes for a living. This is the real gear I actually use

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 19 min read (3756 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Electrek

⏱️ ~19 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that I’m in the somewhat unusual position of basically riding electric bicycles for a living.
  • Of course I don’t just ride e-bikes for work.
  • In other words: I talk the talk and I walk the walk.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that I’m in the somewhat unusual position of basically riding electric bicycles for a living. I’ve been working with e-bikes for nearly two decades, professionally covering the e-bike industry for most of that time, testing hundreds of different models and traveling around the world to ride upcoming e-bikes in some pretty incredible places. Yeah, it’s a tough job – but someone’s got to suffer it.

Of course I don’t just ride e-bikes for work. I ride them recreationally. I ride them for exercise. I ride them for transportation. My family doesn’t even own a car, meaning two wheels handle the vast majority of our transportation.

In other words: I talk the talk and I walk the walk. Or perhaps more accurately, I ride the ride.

And while most of the time all you really need for a good ride is an e-bike and a direction to go in, there are a handful of pieces of gear that I’ve come to rely on over the years. Some keep me safer. Some keep my bikes out of the hands of thieves. Some make rides more comfortable or convenient. And some are just neat little things that I’ve discovered along the way.

Recent findings suggest that this isn’t a list of every bike accessory I’ve ever tested, nor am I saying these are necessarily the absolute best products in every category. These are simply the things that I actually use. Some are a bit pricey, some are dirt cheap (several pieces of gear below are under $5!), but they’re all things I personally rely on and that I recommend to my friends and family. And now, to you.

It has been revealed that if you own nice e-bikes, you’re eventually going to spend a lot of time thinking about locks. Your lock may even be your most crucial accessory. Or perhaps I should say “accessories”, because the best way to ensure your e-bike is still there when you get back is to use more than one solid lock.

My go-to options that I grab basically every day for the last couple of years have been Seatylock’s FoldyLock Forever folding lock and Mason 220 U-lock.

For reference, the Foldylock Forever is the world’s strongest folding lock. That’s not just their marketing speak, but rather it’s confirmed by independent testing and certification. It’s the only folding lock in the world to achieve an ART 3-star security rating awarded by the Stichting ART Foundation, an independent Dutch organization that tests and certifies anti-theft locks. It earned that certification three years ago, and no other folding lock has been able to reach that level yet. The only higher ratings ART gives are for locks rated for motorcycles.

Personally, I like folding locks because they pack relatively neatly on the bike while still giving me enough flexibility to work around different racks and poles, or even larger things like trees.

The FoldyLock Forever is the one I reach for when I want serious security matched with more flexibility, while the Mason 220 gives me another beefy option when I know a U-lock will fit what I’m locking to.

The Mason is great as a strong U-lock, but I also like how large it is, letting me lock to wider poles and also a tad bit farther from the pole itself, leaving room for pannier bags and other things that get in the way. Amazingly, it’s also one of the few U-locks I have that can fit over the beefy battery-filled downtube on most of my e-bikes.

I also use the smaller FoldyLock Compact when I want something easier to carry and don’t need quite as much lock.

It’s more affordable and lighter, though it doesn’t have quite the same security level as the bigger and beefier options above.

Sources indicate that the Compact does have one other advantage, though: it comes in all sorts of bright colors and even a rainbow option where each link is a different color. That might not be a huge security concern, but it’s fun when you can choose a color to match your bike or mood!

Industry observers note that no bike lock makes a bicycle theft-proof. Given enough time and the right tools, a determined thief can defeat virtually anything. The idea is to make your bike enough of a pain in the butt to steal that the thief decides someone else’s bike looks easier. And if they still want your bike (because let’s face it, you’ve probably got an awesome e-bike), then the multiple locks better be good ones so its takes them long enough that they eventually give up.

In a recent development, I also covered Seatylock’s upcoming angle grinder-proof U-locks that I saw at the Milan Motorcycle Show, so I’ll likely switch to those once they come out this Spring. They’re designed to keep motorcycles safe, and come in two sizes: one for motorcycles and a smaller one for bikes.

Let’s continue with what may actually be the most important piece of gear for an e-biker: a helmet.

I’ve tested plenty of helmets over the years, but lately I’ve been gravitating toward UNIT 1’s helmets. They’re comfortable, they look good, and I appreciate the extra safety features beyond simply putting a layer of impact protection around my skull.

I particularly like having integrated lighting built right into my helmet, putting lights up high where they’re easier for drivers to see. On models like the FARO, I also appreciate the inclusion of MIPS as well as the handlebar-mounted remote for activating the helmet’s turn signals.

I recently started using UNIT 1’s NEON helmet too, which is lighter and has a really slick magnetic face shield. You barely have to line the shield up; get it close enough and the magnets practically snatch it out of your hand and put it into place. It’s clear enough for night riding but darkens in bright sunlight, and the helmet is rated for faster 28 mph e-bike riding.

There are cheaper helmets out there, of course, but considering how much time I spend on two wheels, a good helmet is one area where I don’t mind spending a bit more.

You can actually see the FARO helmet in the clip below, along with the TriEye glasses coming up next.

Recent findings suggest that triEye glasses are another accessory that sounds a little gimmicky until you actually start using them. Sunglasses with a built-in rearview mirror? I was sure they were going to be a gimmick but they just looked too interesting to pass up, so I offered to test them out.

Industry observers note that as it turns out, they’re now the first sunglasses I reach for when I’m riding. They really do work!

They have a tiny rear-view mirror integrated into the glasses, giving me a quick view behind me without having to turn my head all the way around.

In a recent development, it takes a little time to get used to looking into such a small mirror, but once your brain figures it out, it becomes surprisingly natural. I can quickly check what’s approaching from behind while still keeping most of my attention pointed forward.

It’s especially useful when riding on roads where I’m regularly interacting with traffic, though I still give an old-fashioned head check before making any major lateral move.

They’re $99, which isn’t bad for decent sunglasses, though you can get them for 10% off with the discount code EBIKE at checkout.

I love listening to music and podcasts while riding, but I’m not a fan of plugging my ears while sharing the road with cars.

That’s why I’ve become a significant fan of H2O Audio’s bone-conduction headphones. They sit outside my ears and transmit sound through bone conduction, meaning my ears themselves remain open to the world around me. I’ve been testing out the latest TRI ULTRA PRO model, and it’s pretty dang amazing! I can hear my music perfectly, but I can still hear all the road sounds, pedestrians, other cyclists, etc.

Of course, that doesn’t mean you can crank the music and magically retain perfect situational awareness. But at reasonable volumes, I can enjoy something in the background while still hearing cars, horns, bells and everything else happening around me.

According to recent reports, for longer recreational rides especially, they’ve become one of those things I really appreciate having along. I’ve done rides as long as 3 hours with them and they haven’t felt cumbersome or made my ears sore, so the fit seems great for me.

According to recent reports, I really like the Knog Oi Prima as a bike bell. It looks good, has a nice low-profile design and does what a bell is supposed to do without looking like you bolted a miniature doorbell onto your handlebars.

Despite its small size, it’s also super loud. And unlike the older ratcheting-style bells (krr-krr-krr-krrring), this is a single thumper, meaning I can ding once quickly for a polite “hello, I’m here!” or several hard and rapid DINGs for a “wtf do you think you’re doing, guy?!”.

The bell absolutely disappears on my handlebars, which is good because there’s not much real estate left up there. Really, the only downside I can find is that it’s not cheap, at around $32 depending on current sales.

But I also have another favorite bell that costs a fraction as much.

I found cheap bike bells on AliExpress that have a hidden compartment for an Apple AirTag. From the outside, it just looks like a boring bike bell. Inside, it’s secretly helping me keep tabs on my bike.

And for $4, they’re a pretty awesome deal for a loud bell that hides a tracking device. Of course, you’ll have to fork over another $20 or so for the AirTag tracker, but your e-bike is certainly worth that much.

Which brings me to another part of my bike security strategy.

It has been revealed that I don’t necessarily stop at one AirTag. One AirTag is for amateurs. I go with multiple. A four-pack is $79, or around half the cost of a solid e-bike lock.

There are all sorts of clever AirTag hiding accessories available now. In addition to the bell, I’ve used a $5 water bottle-style AirTag holder as well as an $8 rear reflector with a hidden AirTag compartment.

According to recent reports, the reflector isn’t the most inconspicuous AirTag hider, but the water bottle holder definitely doesn’t scream “guess what’s actually inside of my molded plastic body!” And for added security, the water bottle holder is held on with Torx bolts. It’s not exactly a security key, but even if a bike thief carries hex wrenches with them, they’re unlikely to have Torx wrenches, meaning that the AirTag will stay on the bike a bit longer while it’s in the hands of a thief.

Industry observers note that airTags aren’t dedicated anti-theft GPS trackers, and Apple intentionally includes anti-stalking features that can eventually alert someone that an unknown AirTag is traveling with them. But I still think they’re a useful additional layer of security, especially because they’re cheap enough to use redundantly.

It has been revealed that A bike thief might know enough to search for an AirTag and remove it. But are they going to keep searching after they find the first one? What about the second? Are they expecting three?

Recent findings suggest that that’s the idea, anyway. And since I keep pretty good tabs on my e-bikes, I’ll know pretty quickly if one goes missing. From there, it’s a race between me getting to the thief and him finding all of my AirTags. Good luck, buddy.

I’m a massive believer in wearing proper protective gear when riding faster electric two-wheelers, but I also don’t particularly want to look like I’m headed to a motorcycle race every time I leave the house. That’s one of the reasons I’ve really come to appreciate my Beyond Riders protective riding hoodie.

Sources indicate that it looks and feels much like a regular casual hoodie, but it’s designed with motorcycle-style protection in mind, including abrasion-resistant materials and removable impact protectors. Believe it or not, there’s flexible CE Level 2 armor in there on the elbows, shoulders, chest, and spine.

I like that I can throw it on before a ride and get an extra layer of protection without having to wear a bulky motorcycle jacket. It’s particularly nice for faster e-bikes and electric mopeds, where the speeds are high enough that I’d rather have something more substantial than a regular sweatshirt between my skin and the pavement.

It has been revealed that of course, no protective hoodie is going to make a crash harmless, and I still choose my gear based on the type of riding I’m doing. But I love products that make it easier to incorporate safety into everyday riding without adding a bunch of hassle. If protective gear is comfortable, convenient, and looks good enough that I actually want to wear it, that’s a big win in my book.

According to recent reports, tannus tire liners are perhaps one of the less exciting products on this list, right up until they save you from fixing a flat on the side of the road. And then they’re the one thing on this list you’ll be ready to open-mouth kiss.

I’ve used Tannus products for years as an extra layer of flat protection, and I’m a major believer in them.

No tire protection system is going to prevent every possible flat, but anything that reduces my chances of sitting on the side of a road pulling a wheel off an e-bike is worth considering.

That’s particularly true with e-bikes, where hub motor wheels can be more complicated to remove thanks to heavy motors, annoying cables, clumsy torque washers, and other hardware.

Tannus tire liners are annoying to install, but you do it once and forget about it. Then you’re almost guaranteed to not get a flat.

And even if you do happen to get a 3″ nail going through it at the perfect angle, they serve as runflats so you can still ride home (albeit a bit slower and more carefully) instead of doing the walk of shame next to your bike.

I don’t want to carry an entire bike shop with me, but I do want enough tools to deal with the common things that can happen during a ride.

The Topeak Ratchet Stick hits a nice sweet spot for me. It’s small enough that I’ll actually bring it along, yet useful enough for the various bolts and adjustments that tend to crop up on bikes.

All of the important bits fit right inside the handle, so I don’t have any extra sleeves or clips to keep tabs on.

This is exactly what I want from a ride tool: something small but effective. The giant tool kit sitting at home isn’t particularly useful when something starts rattling 20 kilometers away.

According to recent reports, at $48, it’s not cheap. But I’ve had mine for around 6 years, and it’s still going strong, so at least it’s well made! At around 8 bucks per year, I’d call it a good investment.

This is one of my more recent cheap finds.

I picked up a waterproof-style pannier bag from AliExpress for around $25, and I’ve been surprisingly impressed with it.

It isn’t quite as substantial as the pannier I have from Priority Bicycles, but it still holds a useful amount of cargo and feels much nicer than I expected for the price.

I particularly like that there are two ways to close it. You can use it as a traditional roll-top pannier and clip the sides together, or you can use the strap that comes over the top when you have too much stuff in there to close it the normal way. I use that second option anytime I have my yoga mat in there since it sticks out the top, but I can still close it relatively tight to keep the mat from swinging around while riding. Depending on how much stuff I’m carrying and how I’ve packed it, having both options is quite convenient.

It’s not the fanciest pannier I own. But for around 25 bucks, it’s one of those cheap accessories that turned out to be much better than I expected.

These might have the highest usefulness-to-price ratio of anything here.

Recent findings suggest that I bought a pair of tiny plastic handlebar jacks on AliExpress for barely more than a dollar. They clip onto the handlebars and provide little stands for when I need to turn a bicycle upside down.

Anyone who has ever flipped a modern e-bike over to change a tube knows the problem. Your handlebars are probably covered in displays, buttons, brake levers, bells, phone mounts and who knows what else. Turning the bike upside down means resting all of that expensive stuff directly on the ground.

In a recent development, you can loosen everything and rotate it out of the way. Or you can use two $1 pieces of plastic.

Recent findings suggest that the jacks hold the handlebars slightly above the ground so my accessories don’t get scratched or crushed. Simple problem, simple solution.

According to recent reports, if you have a 3D printer, you can probably just print your own version of these. There’s a rubber O-ring-style keeper on it, but you can probably just use a rubber band if you wanted to DIY these yourself.

Another recent addition has been a ZOOM suspension dropper seatpost that I installed on my Ride1Up Roadster V3.

I love the thing now that it’s installed. It gives me suspension to take some of the sting out of rough roads while also providing the convenience of a dropper post.

Getting it onto my particular bike, however, was another story.

In a recent development, it took me nearly two hours, largely because the Ride1Up Roadster V3 wasn’t set up for the internal cable routing I needed. I got the cable most of the way there through the downtube’s very narrow wire run, but then I ultimately ended up drilling a small hole in the seat tube to make the last bit of my installation work.

To be very clear: I do not recommend doing that.

Drilling holes in bicycle frames can compromise their structural integrity, void warranties and generally create problems you don’t want. As a mechanical engineer with a lot of bike experience, I was comfortable making that decision on my own bike because I knew exactly where the frame is least stressed, but it’s definitely not something I’d advise others to copy.

Industry observers note that the lesson here isn’t “drill your frame.” It’s to check whether your bike is actually designed for an internally routed dropper post before ordering one. Had I done that first (basically by shining a flashlight down the empty seat tube and realizing there wasn’t a hole to access the bottom bracket), I could have saved myself quite a bit of trouble and just gotten a dropper post with an external cable run.

Recent findings suggest that but now that it’s installed? I love it!

And finally, here’s one that isn’t really normal bike gear at all, but that I LOVE bringing on my rides.

I spend a lot of time taking photos and videos of bikes, which presents an obvious problem when I’m both the cyclist and the photographer.

In a recent development, the HOVERAir X1 Pro Max has become one of my favorite solutions. It’s a tiny autonomous flying camera that can follow me around without requiring someone else to pilot it. I used the previous version of this drone for a while until this version came out, and then I immediately upgraded.

It folds down small enough that I basically forget that I even have it in my bag. Despite its small size, it still can automatically track and follow me, even at speeds of over 20 mph (32 km/h). That means I can pull it out during a ride, send it up (it takes off from my palm!) and get tracking shots that would normally require another person riding or running alongside me with a camera.

I especially like the Dolly Track mode, which can create some fantastic moving shots while automatically following me from the sides or the front, instead of just the boring old follow-behind-me drone shots you usually see.

It has been revealed that just be aware that its obstacle avoidance isn’t great when flying sideways or backward, meaning I’ve flown it into walls, fences, and street signs plenty of times already. But I can also report back that somehow the little guy is still working fine. I’m not suggesting that’s part of the official durability testing procedure, but it has certainly become part of mine. Now it’s my go-to drone, and I especially like bringing it on my travels for all the same reasons.

After a list this long, I should probably point out that you don’t actually need most of this stuff.

According to recent reports, that’s one of the things I love about bikes. You don’t need a pile of expensive gear to have a good time. Most days, give me an e-bike, a helmet and a direction to point the front wheel, and I’m happy.

But after years of riding e-bikes professionally, recreationally, for exercise and simply to get around, these are the products that I’ve found myself continuing to use.

Sources indicate that sure, some of these are expensive pay-to-play things that are a lot of fun but might not be worth it for the casual rider. And some are just $1 pieces of plastic that keep me from smashing my bike computer into the pavement.

But they’ve all found their way into my life after being battle-tested… and passing!

#86947. Latest Update: Wine, beer, or spirits? Massive study reveals a surprising health divide

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1511 w)

General 📈 Bullish 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

Latest Update: Wine, beer, or spirits? Massive study reveals a surprising health divide

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1511 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that A massive study involving more than 340,000 adults has uncovered a surprising difference in the health risks associated with wine, beer, cider, and spirits.
  • Researchers found that low to moderate wine consumption was associated with a lower risk of death, particularly from cardiovascular disease.
  • According to recent reports, the results also reinforce a broader conclusion from previous research: drinking less alcohol is generally better for health.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that A massive study involving more than 340,000 adults has uncovered a surprising difference in the health risks associated with wine, beer, cider, and spirits. Although heavy drinking was linked to worse health outcomes regardless of the beverage, the picture was more complicated among people who consumed smaller amounts of alcohol.

Researchers found that low to moderate wine consumption was associated with a lower risk of death, particularly from cardiovascular disease. In contrast, similar amounts of beer, cider, and spirits were linked to a higher risk. The findings, presented at the American College of Cardiology's Annual Scientific Session (ACC.26), suggest that both the type and quantity of alcohol may influence its relationship with long-term health.

According to recent reports, the results also reinforce a broader conclusion from previous research: drinking less alcohol is generally better for health. Importantly, the fresh findings do not establish that wine itself protects against disease.

"These results come from the general population, and in certain high-risk groups, such as people with chronic diseases or cardiovascular conditions, the risks could be even higher," said Zhangling Chen, MD, PhD, a professor at the Second Xiangya Hospital, Central South University in China and the study's senior author.

How a Study of 340,000 Adults Measured Alcohol Risk.

To investigate the relationship between drinking habits and longevity, scientists examined data from 340,924 adults enrolled in the UK Biobank between 2006 and 2022. The UK Biobank is a large research resource that collects health and lifestyle information to help scientists investigate factors associated with disease and mortality.

Participants reported their alcohol consumption through dietary questionnaires when they joined the study. Researchers then classified them into four groups based on how much pure alcohol they typically consumed each day or week, rather than simply counting drinks.

This distinction matters because beer, wine, and spirits contain different concentrations of alcohol. For comparison, a 12-ounce can of beer, a 5-ounce glass of wine, and a 1.5-ounce shot of spirits each provide approximately 14 grams of pure alcohol.

It has been revealed that people consuming fewer than 20 g (about 1.5 standard drinks) per week were placed in the never or occasional drinking group. Low consumption was defined as 20 g per week up to 20 g per day for men, and 20 g per week up to 10 g per day for women.

In a recent development, moderate drinking was defined as 20 g to 40 g (about 1.5 to three standard drinks) daily for men and 10 g to 20 g daily for women. High consumption meant more than 40 g (about three drinks) per day for men or more than 20 g (about 1.5 drinks) per day for women.

Researchers followed participants' health outcomes for an average of more than 13 years, allowing them to examine how drinking patterns were associated with deaths from different causes.

Wine, Beer, and Spirits Show Different Heart Health Risks.

The clearest finding concerned heavy alcohol consumption. Compared with people who never drank or consumed alcohol only occasionally, heavy drinkers had a 24% higher risk of dying from any cause. Their risk of dying from cancer was 36% higher, while their risk of dying from heart disease was 14% higher.

These increased risks were associated with heavy drinking regardless of whether participants preferred wine, beer, cider, or spirits.

It has been revealed that however, the results became more surprising when researchers examined low and moderate alcohol consumption. At these levels, the type of beverage was associated with substantially different outcomes.

People who consumed wine in low to moderate amounts had a significantly lower risk of death, while those who consumed comparable amounts of beer, cider, or spirits had a significantly higher risk.

The contrast was especially striking for cardiovascular disease, a broad category of conditions affecting the heart and blood vessels. Moderate wine drinkers had a 21% lower risk of dying from cardiovascular disease than people who never or only occasionally drank alcohol.

By comparison, even low consumption of beer, cider, or spirits was associated with a 9% higher risk of cardiovascular death.

Recent findings suggest that these percentages describe relative differences in risk between groups, not the absolute probability that an individual will die from cardiovascular disease. Because the research was observational, the findings also cannot demonstrate that choosing one alcoholic beverage over another directly changes a person's risk.

Recent findings suggest that "Our findings help clarify previously mixed evidence on low to moderate alcohol consumption," Chen said. "These findings can help refine guidance, emphasizing that the health risks of alcohol depend not only on the amount of alcohol consumed, but also on the type of beverage. Even low to moderate intake of spirits, beer, or cider is linked to higher mortality, while low to moderate intake of wine may carry lower risk.".

Why Might Wine Be Linked to Lower Heart Risks?

Researchers identified several possible explanations for the differences, including the chemical composition of wine and the habits of people who drink it.

Industry observers note that red wine contains polyphenols, naturally occurring compounds found in plants that can have antioxidant properties. Antioxidants help counter certain chemical reactions involving unstable molecules that can damage cells. Some polyphenols have been investigated for potential benefits to blood vessels and cardiovascular function.

These compounds could contribute to the associations observed in wine drinkers, although the study did not establish that they were responsible for the lower mortality risk.

Another possible explanation involves how and when people drink.

In a recent development, wine is more commonly consumed alongside meals, and wine drinkers often report healthier diets and lifestyle habits. Drinking wine may therefore be associated with other behaviors that support cardiovascular health.

Beer, cider, and spirits, on the other hand, are more frequently consumed outside of meals. In this study, people who favored these beverages also tended to have poorer overall diet quality and other lifestyle factors associated with increased health risks.

Such differences make it difficult to separate the effects of the alcohol itself from the characteristics and habits of the people consuming it.

"Taken together, these factors suggest that the type of alcohol, how it is consumed, and the associated lifestyle behaviors all contribute to the observed differences in mortality risk," Chen noted.

What the Findings Mean for Alcohol and Health.

To make their comparisons more reliable, the researchers statistically adjusted their analyses for numerous factors that might influence mortality. These included age and other demographic characteristics, socioeconomic circumstances, lifestyle behaviors, and cardiometabolic health.

Sources indicate that cardiometabolic factors include conditions and measurements related to heart and metabolic health, such as blood pressure, blood sugar regulation, and cholesterol levels. The analyses also accounted for family histories of diabetes, cardiovascular disease, and cancer.

Even with these adjustments, the researchers emphasized several notable limitations.

In a recent development, because the study was observational, it could identify associations between alcohol consumption and mortality but could not prove that particular beverages caused better or worse outcomes. Other differences between participants may have influenced the findings despite the statistical adjustments.

In a recent development, alcohol intake was also measured through questionnaires completed when participants first entered the study. That information depended on participants accurately reporting their own drinking habits, and it did not capture changes in consumption during the years that followed.

It has been revealed that another consideration is that UK Biobank participants tend to be healthier than the general population. This could limit how well the findings apply to other groups of people.

Industry observers note that the researchers suggested that high-quality randomized trials could provide stronger evidence about the health effects of different drinking patterns. Such studies would help clarify whether the observed differences reflect the beverages themselves or other factors associated with their consumption.

In a recent development, nevertheless, the enormous study population and more than 13 years of average follow-up provide considerable statistical strength. By examining specific types of alcohol, different levels of consumption, and multiple causes of death, the research offers a more detailed picture of alcohol's potential health risks than many earlier investigations.

The findings highlight an vital distinction: while heavy drinking is consistently associated with harmful health outcomes, the relationships observed at lower consumption levels may depend on beverage choice, drinking habits, and broader lifestyle patterns.

In a recent development, for now, the apparent advantage among wine drinkers should not be interpreted as a reason to start drinking wine for heart health. The evidence points to a complex relationship between alcohol and mortality, rather than proving that any alcoholic drink offers protection.

Ziyue Li presented the study, "Alcohol Use at Mid-Life and All-Cause and Cause-Specific Mortality," at ACC.26.

The 1977 Mazda Cosmo Deserves Better

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (844 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Caranddriver

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that peel the name tags off the Mazda Cosmo, and it could easily pass for an American car.
  • The Cosmo is something of a mystery car.
  • It has been revealed that that’s the situation in the U.S.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

From the April 1977 issue of Car and Driver.

Recent findings suggest that peel the name tags off the Mazda Cosmo, and it could easily pass for an American car. The two-rotor Wankel is as smooth and vibra­tionless as any V-8, the car is easily as quiet inside as a typical intermediate sedan, and the Cosmo’s body even has the same sort of creaky flexibility that we’ve come to expect of Detroit cars. If we didn’t know better, we might think this was a new subcompact Buick or perhaps a miniature Camaro. Never would we confuse it with a Toyota or Datsun.

The Cosmo is something of a mystery car. It was designed with the United States in mind—a fast, smooth sports coupe for a country that swallowed Datsun Z-cars as fast as the ships could unload them at the ports. But for some reason, the Cosmo never struck the American fancy. Maybe it was the bad publicity heaped on the rotary engine; per­haps the dull colors and unfortunate combi­nation of mag wheels and white-wall tires turned off the sporty-car buyer. And we can’t entirely disregard the thought that a coupe with a Vega silhouette, Oldsmobile waterfall grille, and Plymouth Cricket taillights may sim­ply be the wrong thing to wave in American faces. But whatever the reason, Cosmos tend to languish in the showrooms.

See all results for used cars for sale near 84097.

It has been revealed that that’s the situation in the U.S. In Japan, the Cosmo is last season’s smash hit, named Car of the Year by one of the country’s auto mag­azines and the next best thing in Tokyo to driving a foreign car. (The Japanese, like many Americans, tend to think that anything imported is probably better and certainly more fun than the made-at-home equivalent). The car looks great in its own neighborhood. It has slightly different—but not much small­er—bumpers and the mandatory mirrors perched out on the front fenders halfway to the headlights. But apart from those two de­tails, the Japanese-market Cosmo looks the same as the one we tend to ignore here.

We humbly submit, at this point, that the Cosmo deserves another look, if for no other reason than it features one commodity in de­cidedly short supply elsewhere—horsepower. This car is quick. The engine is wide awake above 2000 rpm, and it climbs to 7000 with­out a backward glance. Freeways abound with legions of 350 four-barrels that won’t match the Cosmo’s pace. And as amazing as it may seem, none of them can come close to the Mazda’s gas mileage. The 1977 model with the standard five-speed trans­mission has been weaned down to 32 mpg highway and 20 mpg city for a combined rating of 25 mpg in the EPA mileage sweep­stakes. That is excellent economy for a car of this performance level.

While the Cosmo is surprisingly economical, it is by no means austere. The interior offers about the same amount of useful space for four occupants as a Camaro, and the trunk, because it stows its spare more ef­ficiently than the Chevrolet, is at least as good. Yet overall, the Mazda Cosmo is about the same size as a Corvette, actually slightly smaller.

See all results for used cars for sale near 84097.

Sources indicate that the quality of the interior is also on par with that of Detroit models. The dash is molded vinyl with a minimum of seams, and shows the driver a full complement of instruments set in a field of imitation wood. Velour cloth covers the seats and door panels. There is even a trapezoid opera window to delight the double-knit crowd. And if that doesn’t knock them dead at the Donut Center, show them the wire-spoked steering wheel.

Industry observers note that there is just one aspect of the Mazda’s er­satz Detroit personality with which we take is­sue: It’s a smooth-road car. On ribbons of un­broken concrete the Cosmo simply glides along, but when the going gets rough, so does the ride. The front wheels steer notice­ably over bumps, and the suspension travel is limited enough so that the wheels are occa­sionally jerked clear of the road on surfaces that are not really that rough. The balance of the car, particularly on smooth roads, is rea­sonable however.

In a recent development, at least the Cosmo’s ailments are the kind that can be fixed, certainly by a second look at the factory and perhaps even with a few bolt-on aftermarket parts. We would start with the shocks and see what happens. The rotary engine, on the other hand, is just fine as it is. And Mazda provides an incredible warranty—­five years or 75,000 miles—to make sure it stays that way. Nobody can dislike a car that is guaranteed to keep running even after the loan is paid off.

The Ferrari 296 Challenge Stradale Focuses On the Driver, Strips Out the Hybrid Parts

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that the fresh-for-2026 Ferrari 296 Speciale is a sharper, faster, and more track-oriented variant of the brand’s V-6 supercar—but that doesn’t mean it is the only high-performance variant of the car that Ferrari will build.
  • Recent findings suggest that as the name suggests, the Challenge Stradale is a road-going variant of the 296 that shares a lot in common with the race car currently used in various Ferrari Challenge series.
  • Those components combine to create a massive 1360 pounds of downforce at 155 miles per hour, an increase of 72 percent over the 296 GTB that won Road & Track Performance Car of the Year in 2024.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that the fresh-for-2026 Ferrari 296 Speciale is a sharper, faster, and more track-oriented variant of the brand’s V-6 supercar—but that doesn’t mean it is the only high-performance variant of the car that Ferrari will build. In a somewhat surprising break from recent tradition, Ferrari is also going to make a Challenge Stradale variant of the 296 to sell alongside the Speciale.

Recent findings suggest that as the name suggests, the Challenge Stradale is a road-going variant of the 296 that shares a lot in common with the race car currently used in various Ferrari Challenge series. Specifically, its aerodynamic elements are strikingly similar to the newly introduced 296 Challenge Evo, which was revealed alongside the new road car on November 21. The massive rear wing, front dive planes, and aggressive rear splitter are all extremely similar to design elements seen on that race car.

Those components combine to create a massive 1360 pounds of downforce at 155 miles per hour, an increase of 72 percent over the 296 GTB that won Road & Track Performance Car of the Year in 2024. Downforce is also up 401 lbs at that speed on the 296 Speciale, an increase of 29 percent.

The removal of the hybrid system means a reduction in power, dropping from a combined system output of 819 horsepower in the 296 GTB to an engine-only output of 670 hp in the Challenge Stradale. The simplified powertrain and stripped out interior mean serious reductions in weight to match, though; the Challenge Stradale is 309 lbs lighter than the GTB and 176 lbs lighter than the Speciale.

Industry observers note that does the reduction in weight and increase in downforce make the 296 Challenge Stradale faster than the hybrid 296 Speciale already on the market? Not necessarily. Ferrari claims the Challenge Stradale is half a second a lap faster at its Fiorano test track, but marginally slower at a high-speed circuit like Monza. The more powerful Speciale should be quicker on other tracks with the on-throttle time necessary to allow the hybrid to stretch its legs, while the lighter Challenge Stradale should have the advantage on more technical circuits with more off-throttle time.

The other major differentiation between the Speciale and the Challenge Stradale is availability. While that other high-end 296 variant was a limited-run model, Ferrari stresses that the Challenge Stradale is a part of its regular lineup, and should be more available to buyers. It remains a Ferrari, so the market is unlikely to be flooded with 296s with massive wings in the years to come, but by supercar standards, it should be relatively attainable.

Recent findings suggest that ferrari has not yet announced a price for the American market, but the brand says that it should start at the equivalent of just under $320,000 in Italy, including value-added tax. 📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that are you a port or rail terminal operator looking for a latest electric material handler that can move serious cargo without sacrificing maneuverability? Do you wish it had tank treads? If that’s you, the Mantsinen 200 might be just the thing.

Sources indicate that designed to handle demanding port and rail terminal operations, the Finnish-built Matsinen 200 material handler combines impressive reach and lifting capacity with the ability to move around a worksite on its own tracks. And, yes: I stated tracks.

According to recent reports, by far the most fun feature of the Mantsinen 200 is the fact that it looks like a rejected concept for a ROBOTIX dinosaur set and/or something He-Man would use to run over Trap Jaw. And while, yes – most big material handlers have similar form factors, there’s something about the 200 that really sells the whole Dragon Walker vibe.

The Mantsinen 200 is powered by a 380 kW (~510 hp) grid-connected electric motor running at 1,800 rpm. Power comes from a 460V electrical connection as standard, with other voltage options available to suit local site requirements.

Sources indicate that mantsinen indicates its electrically powered machines deliver the same performance as their diesel counterparts, while eliminating exhaust emissions at the machine and reducing operating noise, energy consumption and maintenance costs. Power is delivered through a load-sensing hydraulic system featuring four variable-displacement piston pumps and a separate closed-loop swing circuit.

In a recent development, mantsinen also fits the 200 with its proprietary HybriLift energy-recovery system. HybriLift works a lot like regenerative braking by capturing potential energy as the main boom is lowered, but instead of storing that energy as electricity in a battery, the material handler stores it in hydraulic accumulators for reuse during the next lift. The organization claims HybriLift improves the massive machine’s energy efficiency by up to 50%, effectively giving the machine an additional 300 (ish) hp of lifting assistance at average lifting speed.

It has been revealed that and, while the machine normally draws power from the grid, operators aren’t necessarily tethered to an outlet. Mantsinen offers an optional PowerPack that allows the machine to disconnect from its main power supply and still travel around the worksite, with some basic hydraulic systems still functional. The PowerPack is currently diesel-powered, but a battery-backed version isn’t out of the question. It’s a useful bit of flexibility for terminal operators who want the benefits of electric material handling without giving up the ability to reposition the machine when a fixed electrical connection isn’t available.

According to recent reports, what do you guys think – is this major material handler the thing you need for your logging or scrapyard, or are you holding out for something even bigger? Let us know in the comments.

Cannabis addiction linked to 57% higher odds of suicidal thoughts

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (948 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, as marijuana becomes more widely available and accepted, researchers are uncovering crucial questions about its effects on mental health.
  • Recent findings suggest that published in the Journal of Studies on Alcohol and Drugs, the research found that adults with cannabis use disorder had 57% higher odds of reporting suicidal thoughts compared with those without the condition.
  • The findings come from an analysis of more than 415,000 American adults who participated in the National Survey on Drug Use and Health.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, as marijuana becomes more widely available and accepted, researchers are uncovering crucial questions about its effects on mental health. A major latest study suggests that people who struggle to control their cannabis use face a substantially greater likelihood of experiencing suicidal thoughts.

Recent findings suggest that published in the Journal of Studies on Alcohol and Drugs, the research found that adults with cannabis use disorder had 57% higher odds of reporting suicidal thoughts compared with those without the condition. Despite major shifts in marijuana laws and public attitudes, this troubling association remained remarkably consistent over a decade.

The findings come from an analysis of more than 415,000 American adults who participated in the National Survey on Drug Use and Health. Researchers examined data collected between 2014 and 2023, a period when cannabis became increasingly accessible across the United States.

According to recent reports, "What surprised me most was not that cannabis use disorder was associated with suicidal thoughts, but that this association did not appear to strengthen over time," mentioned lead author Tosin Philip Oyetunji, MPH, a doctoral student in public health at the University of California, Merced. "[Yet,] it remains an vital mental health concern that deserves attention.".

Cannabis and Suicidal Thoughts Show a Persistent Link.

Recent findings suggest that the connection between cannabis use disorder and suicidal thinking was observed across different age groups, sexes, and racial and ethnic backgrounds. However, women and younger adults indicated particularly elevated risks.

Importantly, the association remained even after researchers accounted for depression, psychological distress, and other factors that could influence mental health outcomes.

According to recent reports, the consistency of the results was especially notable given how dramatically the cannabis landscape has changed. Recreational marijuana is now legal in half of U.S. states, and cannabis products have become increasingly potent. These developments have raised concerns among public health experts about whether broader access might contribute to worsening mental health.

According to recent reports, yet the study offers some reassurance on that particular question. Sidra Goldman-Mellor, PhD, a professor of public health at UC Merced and the study's senior author, noted that the association between cannabis use disorder and suicidal thoughts did not become stronger during the 10 years examined.

It has been revealed that "Suicidal ideation does not seem to have increased among people with cannabis use disorder, despite all this legal and social change," explained Goldman-Mellor. Yet, "people with cannabis use disorder are still at a very substantially increased likelihood of experiencing serious suicidal thoughts, and that's not something that is widely understood.".

Why Cannabis Use Disorder Matters.

The researchers stress that these findings should not be interpreted as evidence that everyone who uses marijuana faces the same elevated risk.

The study focused specifically on cannabis use disorder, a condition in which people have difficulty controlling their marijuana consumption even when it causes problems in their lives. Someone with the disorder may continue using cannabis despite harmful consequences or repeated attempts to cut back.

This distinction is crucial because problematic cannabis use differs from occasional or otherwise nonproblematic consumption.

The findings also do not establish that cannabis use disorder directly causes suicidal thoughts. Because the research identified an association rather than a cause-and-effect relationship, it cannot determine whether problematic cannabis use contributes to suicidal thinking, whether underlying mental health difficulties contribute to both conditions, or whether other factors help explain the connection.

Nevertheless, the results point to a significant mental health concern that deserves greater recognition, particularly among people seeking help for problematic cannabis use.

Researchers Urge Greater Mental Health Screening.

One practical implication is that health care professionals should look beyond cannabis consumption itself when evaluating patients with cannabis use disorder.

Recent findings suggest that rather than focusing exclusively on depression or substance use symptoms, clinicians may benefit from asking patients directly about suicidal thoughts as part of a broader mental health assessment. This could help identify people who need additional care but whose struggles might otherwise remain unnoticed.

In a recent development, "Someone seeking help for cannabis use disorder may also be experiencing suicidal thoughts that are not immediately apparent," noted Oyetunji. "The goal is not to assume that everyone with cannabis use disorder is suicidal but to identify those who may need additional assessment, treatment, or support.".

The study arrives at a time when marijuana is increasingly viewed as a relatively low-risk substance. Public perceptions have shifted considerably, and negative attitudes toward cannabis have declined alongside expanding legalization and social acceptance.

However, these changes have not eliminated the mental health challenges associated with cannabis use disorder. Even though the strength of the association with suicidal thoughts did not increase over the study period, the elevated odds remained substantial.

The researchers suggest that health care providers, policymakers, and community organizations can play an key role by improving awareness, identifying vulnerable individuals, and making appropriate mental health support more accessible.

As attitudes toward marijuana continue to evolve, the findings serve as a reminder that the needs of people experiencing problematic cannabis use should remain a public health priority.

Said Oyetunji, "As cannabis becomes more accessible and socially accepted, we should ensure that the people struggling with its use are not overlooked.".

Waymo Is Recalling Its Robotaxis Because They're Not Great At Dealing With Human Instructions

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (956 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Insideevs

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, waymo recalled its robotaxis again on Friday, citing challenges with navigating closed freeway lanes and handling manually controlled intersections.
  • It has been revealed that the company's robotaxis were banned from California freeways earlier this month after a few high-profile incidents.
  • The robotaxis seem to be very adept at dealing with normal road conditions.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, waymo recalled its robotaxis again on Friday, citing challenges with navigating closed freeway lanes and handling manually controlled intersections. For anyone who has been following Waymo closely, this shouldn't be that surprising.

It has been revealed that the company's robotaxis were banned from California freeways earlier this month after a few high-profile incidents. Waymo took the voluntary step of suspending interstate operation nationwide on Wednesday, meaning the entire fleet is now back to running primarily on local roads and minor state highways.

The robotaxis seem to be very adept at dealing with normal road conditions. But the trouble seems to be when something unexpected pops up. Regulators from California cited poor behavior surrounding closed lanes and construction zones, a recurring issue for the tech giant, along with a another recent high-profile incident involving a California Highway Patrol rolling road block.

Industry observers note that if you don't know what that last sentence means, you aren't alone. When I first moved to California a few years ago, I had no idea what a rolling road block or "traffic break" meant in normal parlance. But drive California freeways long enough and you'll experience one. A CHP cruiser or a group of them joins the highway, puts on its lights, and slowly zigzags across all lanes of traffic, blocking drivers from passing or exceeding the speed of the maneuver. The goal is typically to create a safe break in traffic for authorities to removed debris, clear and accident, or otherwise operate on the road. Sometimes it just slows down the herd before it barrels into a blind-corner accident scene at 80 mph.

When I first experienced this, I was plenty confused. But when I saw cops swerving in front of me with lights on, I naturally just slowed down and stayed behind me. Common sense told me that a cop swerving around with their lights on probably isn't looking for a race. Unfortunately, though, autonomous driving software doesn't always know how to interpret novel situations. So when a Waymo got caught behind a rolling road block, here's what it did:.

Sources indicate that yep, it tried to blow right by. CHP was able to hold it back, but I've seen a Trooper controlling six lanes of traffic with one car before. Add in an inventive and disobedient robotaxi and you can see how it could create a dangerous situation wherein an autonomous vehicle is driving down a road that construction workers or police think is effectively closed.

Now, Waymos are good enough at avoiding hitting things that I don't expect this would have been too bad. But even a small chance of a runaway robotaxi is unacceptable to regulators and to Waymo, so it's good to pause freeway operations until they figure things out.

But the road block situation is indicative of a larger issue with autonomous vehicles, and perhaps the most interesting one. We think of driving as a predominantly legal or process-driven endeavor. You stop at stop signs, obey the speed limit, and keep it between the lines. Errors happen, but we tend to see them as based on improperly applied rules.

In a recent development, yet the police here are disrupting the rules and enforcing an unscheduled and ad-hoc temporary speed limit and traffic flow. If you're from out of state or haven't experienced it yet, it's confusing, as there's direct ruleset for an impromptu situation like that. Yet any other driver caught in this situation wouldn't blow past the cop car. Like me, they'd approach it cautiously, and let the police car take the lead.

That is the glitch I'm referring to: Driving is not just about rules and infrastructure. It's a social behavior. We wave each other ahead at stop signs and intersections. We signal our intent for an aggressive merge by riding the side of the lane market. You look at people's faces to gaze intention and attention. And when the traffic lights are down or the road is blocked by falling trees, we create impromptu order where chaos exists, nodding or waving to signal that it's someone else's term.

It has been revealed that this was always going to be the hard part for robotaxis. That's why the same recall applies to another troubled behavioral pattern for Waymos: They struggle when officers or city workers are manually controlling and intersection. Whether it's due to a high-traffic event or an outage, it's not all that uncommon to see a police officer directing traffic by hand. They wave you through or hold you back.

But what happens if the car loses sight of the person directing traffic? What if the person directing traffic isn't actually a police officer, and waves you through a red light? What if the alternate route the police point you to spits the robotaxi onto a highway, where it isn't allowed to go?

There are a million more what-ifs related to this social component of driving. All of them will have to be encountered and solved as they come, just as you and I eventually figured these things out. Recall by recall, we'll turn these Waymos into upstanding citizens.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Nioh 3 is one of the most anticipated games of 2026, and it’s easily among the biggest releases of February. We’re a few days away from the start of that month, however, but we don’t have to wait until then to actually play Team Ninja’s next major release.

The previously announced demo has arrived, and it’s one any fan of action games should check out, especially if you missed the PlayStation-exclusive beta held last year.

Unlike previous tests, the Nioh 3 demo is available on PC and PS5, just like the main game. This is pretty newly introduced for the series, which has typically rolled out first on PlayStation before coming to PC months later.

It has been revealed that the Nioh 3 demo includes a decent portion of content from the beginning of the game. It’s enough to show off the core duality mechanic, letting you switch between the Samurai and Ninja styles at will. It also includes a preview of the game’s open field level design, which makes it sit somewhere between full open world and the more linear level design of past Nioh games.

Feedback from the previous beta has been implemented into the demo (and full release), so you may see some familiar faces, as well as areas you visited before - assuming you played that one.

Another major reason why you might want to grab the Nioh 3 demo is that your progress in it will carry over to the full version. This includes the character creator, too, meaning you can spend all day perfecting your character without having to worry about missing out on playing the actual game.

In a recent development, the demo even supports online multiplayer for up to three players, in case you come to Nioh for co-op. If you complete the available content, you’ll earn an in-game bonus in the full version. This is something Team Ninja has done with past Nioh titles, of course.

This time, your reward is the Twin-Snake Helmet. Just make sure you complete the demo before February 15.

Nioh 3 is out February 6 on PC, and PlayStation 5.

#86939. Toyota just built a tiny folding electric bike to fit in your trunk

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (852 w)
📖 Baca
EV & Auto ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Electrek ↗ Open Full Page

Toyota just built a tiny folding electric bike to fit in your trunk

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (852 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Electrek

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, toyota is getting into electric bikes.
  • The Japanese automotive giant has unveiled the BKE Concept, a tiny folding electric two-wheeler designed to serve as a compact companion vehicle for short trips, outdoor adventures, and last-mile transportation.
  • In a recent development, and when Toyota indicates compact, it means it.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, toyota is getting into electric bikes. Well, sort of.

The Japanese automotive giant has unveiled the BKE Concept, a tiny folding electric two-wheeler designed to serve as a compact companion vehicle for short trips, outdoor adventures, and last-mile transportation.

In a recent development, and when Toyota indicates compact, it means it. The little electric ride can reportedly fold up in around 30 seconds and become small enough to fit inside the trunk of the brand’s GR86 sports car. Think of it like Toyota’s take on the Motocompacto.

The BKE Concept was unveiled as part of the newly revived Scion by Toyota brand, which the firm is positioning less as the return of the quirky youth-oriented car brand many Americans remember and more as a sort of experimental mobility laboratory.

Recent findings suggest that toyota calls the fresh Scion a “freedom lab” where the company can explore vehicles and mobility concepts that don’t necessarily fit neatly into its conventional automotive lineup. Alongside the BKE, Toyota showed its KEI-01 ultra-compact utility truck and a hybrid side-by-side.

But perhaps unsurprisingly for me, it’s the tiny electric two-wheeler that caught my attention.

Recent findings suggest that and I should point out here that while Toyota refers to it as an “electric bike” in its own brand literature, the lack of pedals means that the cute little two-wheeler is not going to qualify as an electric bicycle in Europe or North America. The moniker means it merely slots into the broader electric bike category that encompasses everything from electric bicycles to scooters and motorcycles. In essence, the BKE is more or less a small seated e-scooter, sometimes referred to as a “no-ped”.

Despite looking like the kind of concept vehicle that might have been whipped up for an auto show, Toyota says the BKE has actually been under development for several years.

A small team of chassis and electrical engineers has reportedly been testing and refining the design based on real-world use and feedback.

The basic idea came from a fairly simple question: How could Toyota make short-distance mobility easier and integrate it more seamlessly into everyday life?

The result is essentially a secondary vehicle designed to travel inside your primary vehicle.

Toyota specifically highlights camping, errands, last-mile transportation, and even using the BKE as a pit bike alongside a GR86. The bike can also be recharged from the 110V AC outlets found in many Toyota vehicles, meaning the car carrying it can effectively serve as its mobile charging station.

Believe it or not, Toyota Chairman Akio Toyoda has apparently been involved in the testing process himself. Toyoda attracted attention after riding a similar small electric mobility device around the 2025 Japan Mobility Show, and Toyota claims his experience riding prototypes has even resulted in design changes.

After Toyoda complained about getting splashed while riding through puddles, for example, engineers enlarged the rear fender.

It’s a small detail, but it’s also a pretty textbook example of Toyota’s famous kaizen philosophy of continuous improvement.

Here’s where things get a little frustrating for those of us who want to know what the BKE can actually do.

Recent findings suggest that toyota hasn’t announced the motor power, battery capacity, range, top speed, or even the vehicle’s weight. There’s also no pricing because, for now, there’s nothing to buy.

Toyota is referring to the BKE strictly as a concept and hasn’t confirmed production aims or a timetable for bringing it to market.

But the fact that Toyota indicates a small engineering team has spent several years developing and testing the BKE makes it more interesting than your typical one-off styling exercise.

And the underlying idea makes a lot of sense.

I’m obviously a significant believer in matching the vehicle to the trip. Taking a 4,000-pound car several miles to move one person isn’t always the most efficient solution, and a compact electric two-wheeler gives drivers an easy way to leave the larger vehicle behind for those shorter trips.

Toyota itself makes essentially the same argument, saying that using smaller vehicles for shorter journeys could reduce emissions by better matching the vehicle to the task.

There’s also something amusingly circular about one of the world’s largest automakers arriving at the conclusion that sometimes the best vehicle for a trip is a tiny electric bike.

But hey, I’ll take it. Now Toyota just needs to actually build the thing – and preferably tell us how fast it goes first.
